articles.title: Luka Dončić-led Lakers begin post-LeBron James era with blowout win over Warriors
articles.summary: Luka Dončić and Walker Kessler both had big games.
articles.body:
For the first time since 2017, the Los Angeles Lakers began their season without LeBron James on the roster. But they still have Luka Dončić.

That was more than enough for their season opener on Wednesday, a 127-105 home win over the short-handed Golden State Warriors.

Dončić certainly looked eager to define this Lakers era, posting 28 points on 7-of-18 shooting, 8 rebounds, 7 assists and 3 steals. He spent much of the game matched up against Warriors rookie Yaxel Lendeborg and appeared to take the assignment personally. He repeatedly went after the No. 12 pick of the 2026 NBA Draft and let him know about it after the play.

That included on a half-court shot to end the first half, pointing at Lendeborg after the buzzer.

That's something of a "Welcome to the NBA" moment for Lendeborg, who won an NCAA championship and All-American honors last season at Michigan.

So Dončić appears ready to keep doing his thing without James. As for the other Lakers, trade acquisition Walker Kessler had a big Lakers debut with 26 points on 12-of-12 shooting. His 10 dunks were the most by a Laker in a single game since a big man by the name of Shaquille O'Neal in 2003.

Dončić assisted on five of those dunks, forming the kind of two-man game when the Lakers had in mind when they gave the big man a four-year, $130 million sign-and-trade deal .

The new-look defense made life tough for the Warriors, who are without Jimmy Butler, Kristaps Porziņģis and Moses Moody to open the season. Stephen Curry led the group with 23 points, but Golden State shot only 27 of 70 as a team before emptying out its bench at the start of the fourth quarter.

The sour note for the night was a painful-looking injury for Jake LaRavia, a returnee expected to get rotation minutes this season. He appeared to roll his ankle on a drive during garbage time.

It was a transformative season overall for the Lakers. Among the nine Lakers players to see pre-garbage-time minutes on Wednesday only three members were part of the Lakers last season: Dončić, Austin Reaves and LaRavia.

James is gone. Marcus Smart is gone. Rui Hachimura is gone. DeAndre Ayton, Luke Kennard and Jaxson Hayes are all gone. The Lakers responded by bringing in the likes of Kessler, Matisse Thybulle and Ziaire Williams, who all started against the Warriors, plus Quentin Grimes, Sandro Mamukelashvili and Kevon Looney, who came off the bench.

There aren't many places bullish on the idea of this group doing what the James-led group couldn't in his last few years in Los Angeles, but the transformation was likely inevitable once Dončić came to town. This is now a team built entirely around the 27-year-old, with the ability to try building for beyond this season.

Wednesday at least represents a good start in that regard.

articles.title: Lakers Beat Warriors Box Score Stats, Highlights for Steph Curry, Luka Doncic, Kessler, Top Players
articles.summary: The Los Angeles Lakers crushed the Golden State Warriors 127-105 in their regular season opener on Wednesday in L.A.
articles.body:
The Los Angeles Lakers crushed the Golden State Warriors 127-105 in their regular season opener on Wednesday in L.A.

The Lakers, who were 6.5-point favorites (per FanDuel Sportsbook ), featured six new players in their nine-man rotation. This was also their first game since LeBron James, who played eight seasons in town, left in free agency for the Philadelphia 76ers.

L.A. gets a glowing early review for its first effort. Here's a look at some notable box score stats.

Warriors, Heat, More on Wrong Side of NBA History With Rare Stat After Blowout Losses in Openers

The highlight of the game was Luka Dončić's half-court buzzer beater to give L.A. a 66-52 halftime edge.

That shot capped a 32-19 second quarter. L.A. poured it on in the third, outscoring Golden State 36-16. All told, it was Los Angeles 68, Golden State 35 over the second and third quarters, and that put the Lakers up front 102-68 going into the fourth.

Lakers center Walker Kessler arrived in town this offseason via a sign-and-trade with the Utah Jazz and signed a four-year, $130 million deal . He began his Laker tenure by shooting a perfect 12-of-12 from the field, helping L.A. dominate the paint and make 57 percent of its field goals.

The Luka-Kessler combination was working, to say the least.

Austin Reaves re-signed with the Lakers for four years and $185 million, and he began his new deal with a solid 23-point outing on just 11 shots (10-of-10 from the line).

Meanwhile, this was not a good night for Golden State.

Rookie Yaxel Lendeborg, the No. 11 overall pick in the NBA draft, did impress at times and showed why he should be in the Rookie of the Year conversation.

He and Dončić also trash talked in this one. Lendeborg got a technical for his efforts.

The Warriors also got off to a great start, with Stephen Curry scoring 16 first quarter points.

However, it was all downhill from there.

Both teams play at home on Friday evening. L.A. will remain in town to host the Los Angeles Clippers. Golden State will look to rebound on Friday vs. the Memphis Grizzlies.

articles.title: Doncic lidera la paliza a los Warriors, encuentra un nuevo socio y cumple una promesa en su estreno
articles.standfirst: El base abre el curso con 28+8+7 y estrena sociedad con el pívot Walker Kessler: 26 puntos con 12/12 en tiros de campo
articles.summary: El base abre el curso con 28+8+7 y estrena sociedad con el pívot Walker Kessler: 26 puntos con 12/12 en tiros de campo
articles.body: Antes del debut de los Lakers en la temporada NBA, Luka Doncic compró una página entera en el diario 'Los Angeles Times'. Era para publicar un mensaje hacia la ciudad y los aficionados de la franquicia. "Todo jugador sueña con levantar ese trofeo. Hacerlo por todos ustedes, nuestros increíbles aficionados, significaría muchísimo para nosotros. Tenemos un equipo especial. Sabemos lo que esperan y haremos todo lo que esté en nuestras manos para cumplirlo. Así que aquí está mi promesa: les daremos todo lo que tenemos, cada noche. Sin excusas. Sin noches libres", podía leerse. En el estreno del año I después de LeBron James, el base y los Lakers cumplieron su promesa. Le dieron una paliza a los Warriors: 127-105. Doncic, en su primer partido desde el 2 de abril, fue el mejor con 28 puntos (7/18 en tiros de campo incluido un 5/12 en triples), ocho rebotes y siete asistencias. Su borrón, las seis pérdidas. En el último cuarto no jugó. Con él en pista, +31 para su equipo. Su socio habitual, Austin Reaves llegó a los 23 puntos. Pero el esloveno ha encontrado uno nuevo un Walker Kessler, llegado este verano desde los Jazz. Y su sociedad promete. El pívot, en su estreno con los Lakers, acabó con 26 puntos y nueve rebotes. Bestial 12/12 en tiros de campo. Sólo otro jugador de los Lakers metió tantos lanzamientos sin fallo: Wilt Chamberlain, que hizo 14/14 en 1969 en un partido ante los Pistons. Diez de las canastas de Kessler fueron mates, algo que, como 'laker' sólo había conseguido Shaquille O'Neal. Muchas llegaron después de asistencias de Doncic, que probablemente nunca en su carrera NBA haya disfrutado de un jugador interior así. Entre los dos se pueden poner las botas en una conexión que funciona desde el primer momento dada la facilidad del base para encontrar a un pívot con gran facilidad para acabar por encima del aro. Lo que fue el partido duró hasta cerca del descanso. El primer cuarto fue igualado (34-33). Doncic asistió a Kessler para que machacara en la primera canasta del choque anticipando lo que sería la noche. En la primera pausa, el pívot ya sumaba ocho puntos y tres mates. El base había clavado un par de triples. Stephen Curry daba la réplica con un buen arranque. Después se frenaría y acabaría con 23 puntos y 2/7 en triples. Dada la diferencia en el marcador sólo jugó 21 minutos. Los Warriors no pudieron contar con Brandin Podziemski , Jimmy Butler, Moses Moody y un Kristaps Porzingis que está meditando su retirada con sólo 31 años. Al descanso el marcador era de 66-52 después de que Doncic metiera un triple a tablero desde medio campo. Se lo dedicó al novato Yaxel Lendeborg, con el que tuvo varios piques e intercambios de palabras. "Llegué con mucho respeto por Luka, pero todo se fue por la forma en que se queja durante todo el partido", dijo el jugador de los Warriors. Al inicio de la segunda parte, el encuentro se desintegró. El parcial de 36-16 lanzó a los angelinos a un triunfo plácido. Llegaron a ganar por 35 puntos, aunque hubo relajación en el cuarto final, ya con Doncic descansando en el banquillo. En su primer partido, los Lakers cumplieron la promesa del base, aunque estos Warriors no son unidad de medida. "Es sólo el primer partido. Creo que nuestro techo es aún más alto", dijo el esloveno.

articles.title: Behind raucous home crowd, Angel Reese, Dream make statement in commanding Game 3 win vs. Valkyries: 'Y'all not taking this from us'
articles.summary: The Dream's Game 1 loss pissed Angel Reese off, and she's been playing like she's got something to prove ever since.
articles.body:
ATLANTA — Angel Reese thrives on perceived disrespect. The mere mention of that to her is disrespectful. She turns, her face shutting off, an "I don't care" signaling the end of a one-on-one conversation toward the end of shootaround.

But she does care. Or else she wouldn't drop an aside that the goals she wrote down at the beginning of the season were ones "that many people may not think I can do." A shiny new Defensive Player of the Year trophy sat beside her on a black-clothed table.

Or that "nobody wants [the] Atlanta Dream in it" on the eve of what would become a semifinals sweep of the New York Liberty. Not if it didn't linger with her. Not if it wasn't what she herself called a chip on her team's shoulder, an ordinary if not overused motivator used by the greatest in the world.

Reese is not immune. She lifted LSU to its first NCAA national championship as a squad of overlooked transfers that didn't face top competition until the tournament. Tigers head coach Kim Mulkey attended Game 3 at State Farm Arena in Atlanta on Wednesday, delivering an embrace and telling her star to go get it again.

She's in a similar role as the imperative offseason addition, the motor to the previously built bus that finally clicked back on every offensive cylinder in a 97-71 win over the Golden State Valkyries . The Dream lead the series 2-1 and are halfway to the title, as Dream head coach Karl Smesko astutely pointed out, with Game 4 back at State Farm on Saturday (1 p.m. ET).

In her first WNBA Finals, Reese and the Dream disrespected themselves. Despite leading late on the road inside the most consistently intense arena in the WNBA, they let a victory slip by in the final minutes . They didn't play their style, and were exposed in the process. The franchise dropped to 0-10 in Finals games.

"As soon as she stepped on the court, she was like, I'm going to be the best player on that court tonight," DeWanna Bonner, the Dream's August signing, said ahead of shootaround of Reese's Game 2 performance .

She did it again in Game 3. With 21 points and 12 rebounds, Reese became the youngest player in Finals history with at least 20 points and 10 rebounds in consecutive games and only the second after three-time Las Vegas Aces champion A'ja Wilson. She also became the youngest, at 24 years old, with three straight double-doubles in the Finals. In Game 3, she added three assists and three steals, shooting 7 of 12 including both of her 3-point attempts and all five free throws.

"Angel shows up in every game," point guard Jordin Canada, a two-time champion, said. "Some people only show up at big games, but she's consistent with that, and she brings her teammates along."

Four of the five Atlanta starters scored double digits, joined by Rhyne Howard (16 points), Naz Hillmon (15) and Canada (10), who moved into first all-time in Dream career assists. Allisha Gray had eight points with six assists. Isobel Borlase added 12 off the bench, now tied for first in franchise postseason points for a rookie. Atlanta shot 49.3% from the floor, opening the basket in a way neither team had managed to over the first two games, which never cracked 33%. They were 9 of 22 from 3, with the Valkyries going 12 of 30.

Reese (who else?) laid in the game's first bucket to kick off the ugliest start to any game of the series, their defensive-minded approaches taken into consideration. The Valkyries didn't score until the 5:07 mark, on a free throw, and didn't make their first bucket until 4:38. It was the second-longest drought to open a Finals game of all time, per Elias.

She scored a team-high eight points in the first quarter of a 23-15 game. Once the offenses delivered a back-and-forth affair, she hit all three field goal attempts for seven points with four rebounds and a 46-40 lead.

The real Dream work happens in the third quarter, where they are 63-35 in this series. The Valkyries tied the game for a total of one minute early in the third before the Dream snatched it away for good and left nothing to doubt.

Reese stared down the Valkyries on the bench, yelling "she can't f*** with me" when she scored over Valkyries rookie center Aminata Gueye. She swatted shots, snatched rebounds and stomped the floor with a flex. Though she has said she likes the intimacy of the Dream's standard 3,500-seat Gateway Center Arena, a sold-out 17,099 at State Farm, where there are as many in-game performances as Reese quips to opponents, suits her.

Between the lines and the buzzer is where Reese does her talking. To thread a conversation with her otherwise can be as tricky as side-stepping through her in the paint or battling her on the boards for a rebound. Or, increasingly, guarding her at the 3-point line.

It cannot be understated that her improved perimeter game has lifted the third-year forward into a new stratosphere, and served as a key contributor to the Dream's run at the franchise's first championship. She hit two more in Game 3, lifting the team's record to 15-0 when she drills from the arc.

The Valkyries could fight back all they wanted. That hesitation and drilled open, 25-foot look by Reese with 40.1 seconds left in the first quarter essentially sealed their fate. The second glued it completely shut. The crowd lifted and met her own roar, a crescendo of energy from everyone in blue.

"When you have a mentality that started from me, where I'm hype all the time and bringing the confidence into everybody, y'all not taking this from us," Reese said. "And in my heart, I'm not letting you take this from us."

Reese is the type of player you're glad is on your side and not the other. The one who wants all the smoke, and will serve as her own fog machine when needed. In the end, it won't matter how or what perceived slight or claim brought her here. Two victories from lifting the championship trophy, Reese is well on her way to proving the doubters wrong.

articles.title: Una NBA sin prioridad nacional
articles.summary: La opinión de Jesús Sánchez
articles.body: Aday Mara le puso un tapón por encima del aro a Wembanyama en sus primeros minutos en la NBA. El pívot aragonés no sólo lucía en el 'prime time' de la competición con una jugada que alimentaba el relato como kryptonita del francés. Fue una magnífica tarjeta de presentación y de alguna manera venía a confirmar por un lado que este chico de Zaragoza tiene estrella y que la trascendencia de los jugadores internacionales es imparable desde el minuto uno. La notoriedad obedece a la cantidad y la calidad, y también un cambio de actitud a la hora de reclutar. La NBA se quitó el gorro de cowboy y abrió un buen día sus puertas al mundo. Un total de 125 jugadores no estadounidenses de 450 posibles iniciarán la temporada 81ª de la competición profesional de baloncesto. Francia aporta 17 y Canadá, que ha liderado estos años, 16. España, después de unas temporadas sin demasiada relevancia, tendrá cinco: Hugo González, Mara, Baba Miller, Aldama y De Larrea. Un total de 43 países distintos (igual el récord de la campaña 2017-18) están representados en la NBA, competición que se puede ver por televisión en 214 países. Obviamente no se juega tan buen baloncesto en los cinco continentes, hay muchos niveles, pero la capilaridad de la marca NBA por todo el planeta convierte el campeonato norteamericano en la Liga de baloncesto del mundo. Sólo Europa, devoto de un juego más ortodoxo y rico a la vez, aporta 71. En 1985, sólo aparecía el búlgaro Glouchkov. Después llegarían Fernando Martín y otros muchos. El número de europeos, tratándose del Viejo Continente donde hay un fantástico trabajo en la formación de jugadores y una devoción por la tradición en el juego, no es tan sorprendente como los 60 jugadores africanos o de origen africano que empezarán la NBA 2026-27. ¿Prevalencia del físico? Nigeria, 52 en el ranking de la FIBA, aporta seis. Olajuwon fue precisamente una de las primeras estrellas internacionales del campeonato. Alemania, campeona del mundo, tiene siete. Australia, nueve. Lo que pudo parecer hace años una tendencia, a raíz de la explosión estelar de jugadores como Ginobili, Nowitzki, Parker o Pau Gasol que siguieron la estela de Kukoc, Divac, Smits, Petrovic o Sabonis, se ha convertido en un patrón. La excepción es la regla. Es la sexta temporada consecutiva con 120 internacionales o más. En la temporada 2025-26 la cota se fijó en 135. Dallas Mavericks, Miami Heat y Washington Wizards tienen siete cada uno. Lo que puede parecer una colosal torre de Babel es riqueza porque además últimamente los jugadores más valiosos ya no son estadounidenses. En los últimos cinco años, los tres primeros en la carrera por el premio al jugador más valioso han sido internacionales. En 2026, Shai, Jokic y Wembanyama. El escolta de los Thunder lleva dos años como MVP. Cuatro jugadores no estadounidenses han ganado el trofeo en las ocho últimas temporadas (Shai, Jokic, Embiid y Antetokounmpo). Estados Unidos no levanta el trofeo desde James Harden en 2018. Según las encuestas entre los directores deportivos, el francés Wemby y el serbio Jokic son los candidatos a ganar en 2027 y el prodigio francés el favorito como ‘jugador franquicia’ a la hora de construir un equipo de cero. Y Wemby definitivamente marca tendencia. Porque en la NBA, tal y como evoluciona la selección de personal, el jugador típico es paradójicamente el que resulta imposible de tipificar, el hombre al que no puedes atar a una posición, capaz de hacer muchas cosas bien, como Doncic, Anteto, Jokic o el marciano francés…

articles.title: Baba Miller, vigesimosegundo español en la NBA, muestra su hambre en su debut
articles.standfirst: El alero se estrena con los Clippers con un mate descomunal: cuatro puntos y tres rebotes en nueve minutos, su primera estadística
articles.summary: El alero se estrena con los Clippers con un mate descomunal: cuatro puntos y tres rebotes en nueve minutos, su primera estadística
articles.body: Y ya son 22 los jugadores españoles que han disputado algún partido en la NBA. El último en estrenarse ha sido Baba Miller. El alero mallorquín de 22 años y 2,09 metros ha debutado con los Clippers durante el cómodo triunfo sobre los Kings por 121-96. En los nueve minutos en que ha estado en pista, ha sumado cuatro puntos (2/2 en tiros de campo), tres rebotes y una asistencia. Miller dejó una de las jugadas de la noche cuando, a falta de siete minutos para el final del encuentro y con todo ya decidido, recibió un pase en bote de su compañero Darius Garland, que fue el mejor del choque con 30 puntos. Tras el bloqueo y continuación, el español, en lo alto de la zona, vio el camino libre hacia el aro de los Kings y culminó la acción con un mate tremendo. Marca de la casa y muestra del hambre que tiene en su primer curso en la NBA. El internacional español pudo disfrutar de un placentero triunfo para arrancar su carrera en la Liga profesional. Los Clippers no tuvieron problema para imponerse a los Kings desde el inicio. El 41-29 del primer cuarto ya fue un aviso. El 32-16 del tercer periodo terminó de romper el choque. Domantas Sabonis, con 14+18, y Zach LaVine, con 28 puntos, fueron los más destacados en las filas de Sacramento.

articles.title: El Real Madrid va cogiendo ritmo
articles.standfirst: Los blancos persiguen en la visita al Maccabi Tel Aviv su séptima victoria consecutiva, cuarta en la Euroliga
articles.summary: Los blancos persiguen en la visita al Maccabi Tel Aviv su séptima victoria consecutiva, cuarta en la Euroliga
articles.body: Seis victorias consecutivas, tres de ellas en la Euroliga, han hecho que el Real Madrid vaya cogiendo vuelo. La filosofía de Pedro Martínez cada vez está más asentada en la plantilla: rebote (han ganado esa batalla en 11 de 12 encuentros oficiales), velocidad, juego coral (en los últimos cuatro partidos han anotado los 12), compartir el balón (59 asistencias en los dos últimos), acierto exterior (tres citas seguidas por encima del 40%)... Baloncesto total, en definitiva: 144,0 de valoración media en los cuatro duelos de la última semana. Bajo esos preceptos, los blancos esperan este jueves (20.05 horas) mantener su buena dinámica en su visita al Maccabi Tel Aviv, todavía en el exilio de Belgrado. Si consiguen el objetivo, al acabar esta séptima jornada tendrían más triunfos que derrotas por primera en la temporada europea. En un baloncesto de marcadores elevados, el Madrid marca tendencia. Se nota la mano de su técnico. “Ahora mismo, en la ACB y también en Europa, se juega a posesiones cortas, buscar ventaja rápido, jugar con alta intensidad alta… Personalmente, es un tipo de baloncesto en el que me siento a gusto, pero no hay una manera única de jugar bien”, analiza el entrenador, que se pregunta “cuánto tiempo va a durar esto, porque el deporte está en constante evolución y seguramente los equipos que no quieran jugar a ese ritmo harán cosas, se adaptarán y generarán problemas”. La última semana del Madrid es un claro ejemplo del baloncesto que se hace en la actualidad: 112 puntos de media en los cuatro encuentros disputados. “Creo que vamos por el buen camino, pero no podemos conformarnos con la racha de victorias. Queremos seguir progresando, seguir mejorando y ganando partidos”, afirma Theo Maledon, uno de los referentes del equipo madridista. El equipo tuvo claro desde la pretemporada a qué quería jugar. Otra cosa es que el rival se lo permitiera. En esa guerra por marcar el tempo de los partidos, el Madrid está ganando últimamente. Ante el Maccabi espera seguir haciéndolo. “Tenemos que imponer nuestro juego, nuestro estilo: jugar rápido, con mucha intensidad, asegurar el rebote… Eso va a ser importante”, considera Maledon. Martínez también agradece el esfuerzo de los jugadores por asumir su manera de entender el baloncesto: “No es fácil adaptarse a jugar y producir menos a cambio de que el equipo sea mejor”. Y tiene palabras para quienes menos juegan, como Shulga o Llull: “Como entrenador, no puedo estar pendiente de si un jugador juega mucho o poco. Mi responsabilidad es con todo el equipo. Intento que todos estén con confianza, que se sientan importantes y ya veremos cómo va la temporada. Todos los jugadores que tenemos, si jugaran más minutos, harían mejores estadísticas”.

articles.title: Dos entrenadores españoles en el derbi de Belgrado: "El Clásico es un juego de niños comparado con esto"
articles.standfirst: Joan Peñarroya, técnico del Partizan, e Ibon Navarro, su homólogo en el Estrella Roja, se enfrentan este jueves en uno de los partidos más calientes del baloncesto europeo
articles.summary: Joan Peñarroya, técnico del Partizan, e Ibon Navarro, su homólogo en el Estrella Roja, se enfrentan este jueves en uno de los partidos más calientes del baloncesto europeo
articles.body: El equipo del ejército, frente al equipo del pueblo. El Partizan, frente al Estrella Roja. El derbi eterno, como se conoce al duelo entre los dos grandes equipos de Belgrado. Este jueves se disputa uno de los encuentros más calientes que pueden verse en el baloncesto europeo. Y en cada banquillo, en una situación sorprendente, dos entrenadores españoles. En el infierno del Belgrado Arena estarán Joan Peñarroya e Ibon Navarro. Y como árbitro, otro español, Carlos Peruga. El primero, que dirige al Partizan desde diciembre del año pasado, ya sabe lo que va a vivir. "He tenido la suerte de vivir los Madrid-Barça, que son un partido especial, pero, aunque quede mal decirlo, eso es un juego de niños comparado con esto. Aquí es otra cosa", asegura Peñarroya durante una charla con MARCA. "Tiene el componente de que son dos equipos de la misma ciudad, algo que no pasa en los Clásicos. Belgrado está dividida y se vive la previa, los días antes, los días posteriores... Es un partido que vale como cualquier otro, pero allí vale mucho más", añade el técnico catalán. El Partizan anunció este martes que, como siempre de cara al derbi, se habían agotado las entradas. Más de 20.000 espectadores poblarán las gradas del Belgrado Arena. La temporada pasada, en este mismo duelo, hubo 21.854. "La atmósfera es muy diferente. Es una maravilla tener la suerte de vivir un partido de esas características. Fue una de las razones que a me motivaban cuando decidí venir a Belgrado: vivir una experiencia así. Es un partido muy chulo y con una presión enorme para todos", explica. Enfrente, Ibon Navarro, que en una semana de máxima intensidad no ha querido exponerse ante los medios más que a lo que le obliga la Euroliga. Tiene muy buena relación con Peñarroya, pero no ha habido consejos. Mejor que se tope con un ambiente que, en su caso, será hostil. "Seguro que va con la lección aprendida. Todos los que nos dedicamos a esto ya hemos visto lo que son estos partidos en Belgrado, pero luego hay que vivirlo", admite el entrenador del Partizan. Pese a lo bien que se llevan, los dos técnicos españoles no se ven en Belgrado. Tampoco sus agendas favorecen un encuentro, pero es que no se cita ni para un café. "No se vería bien que los entrenadores de Partizan y Estrella Roja quedaran. Si quieres salir en las noticias y abrir todos los telediarios...", bromea Peñarroya. "Nuestra relación no va a cambiar, pero nuestro máximo rival es el Estrella Roja y el suyo somos nosotros. Así que ya quedaremos en verano. Si nos vemos en Málaga o se viene para Barcelona, hablamos tranquilamente", finaliza.

articles.title: Haliburton vuelve 486 días después y los Wizards están en positivo por primera vez en cuatro años
articles.standfirst: El base de los Pacers suma 23 puntos y 12 asistencias en su primer partido tras superar una rotura del tendón de Aquiles y acaba entre lágrimas
articles.summary: El base de los Pacers suma 23 puntos y 12 asistencias en su primer partido tras superar una rotura del tendón de Aquiles y acaba entre lágrimas
articles.body: Tyrese Haliburton fue uno de los grandes protagonistas de la jornada. El base de los Pacers volvió a jugar después de 486 días por la lesión del tendón de Aquiles sufrida en las finales de 2025 y firmó 23 puntos y 12 asistencias en la victoria de los Indiana Pacers por 123-120 en el campo de los New Orleans Pelicans. El base se emocionó al finalizar el encuentro al pensar en su largo proceso de recuperación. "Significa mucho estar de vuelta", dijo entre lágrimas después del encuentro. Anthony Davis estrenó su etapa con los Washington Wizards con 34 puntos, 12 rebotes y 4 asistencias en la victoria por 128-116 ante los Milwaukee Bucks. Con este triunfo, la franquicia de la capital está con un récord positivo (un simple 1-0, eso sí) por primera vez desde el 28 de noviembre de 2022. Han pasado 1.423 días. Sus 34 puntos igualaron la mejor marca anotadora en un debut con Washington, establecida por Antawn Jamison en 2004. Davis convirtió 11 de sus 20 tiros de campo y 11 de sus 14 lanzamientos libres. Sin AJ Dybantsa, primera elección absoluta en el último draft, Trae Young acompañó al pívot con 20 puntos y 13 asistencias. Los Bucks tuvieron como máximos anotadores a Tyler Herro, con 24 puntos y 9 asistencias, y el mexicano Jaime Jaquez Jr., con 22 puntos y 7 rebotes. Kawhi Leonard regresó a Toronto, donde conquistó el campeonato de 2019, con 23 puntos y seis rebotes en la victoria de los Raptors por 135-92 ante los Chicago Bulls. Leonard compartió el liderato anotador con Scottie Barnes e Immanuel Quickley, ambos con 23 puntos. RJ Barrett contribuyó con 20 en un triunfo por 43 puntos de diferencia que marcó el debut del brasileño Tiago Splitter como entrenador de Chicago. Los Brooklyn Nets del técnico español Jordi Fernández también perdieron, en su caso en casa, por 110-103 ante los Charlotte Hornets. Grayson Allen lideró a Charlotte con 21 puntos y 5 triples, Naz Reid sumó 20 puntos, 11 rebotes y 7 asistencias y Dennis Schroder aportó 19 puntos. Brooklyn no pudo aprovechar los 33 puntos, 8 rebotes y 7 asistencias de Julius Randle.

articles.title: WNBA Finals: Angel Reese stars again as Atalanta Dream beat Golden State Valkyries to move 2-1 up in best-of-seven series
articles.summary: Atlanta Dream take lead in WNBA Finals at 2-1 in best-of-seven series as they secure 97-71 home win vs Golden State Valkyries; Angel Reese again proves the standout with 21 points and 12 rebounds; Game 4 takes place on Saturday; watch WNBA Finals live on Sky Sports
articles.body:
Rhyne Howard added 16 points and Naz Hillmon had 15 for the Dream, who host Game 4 on Saturday.

It was the second straight strong game for Reese, who had 30 points and 16 rebounds in Game 2, which the Dream also won for their first victory ever in the finals. She becomes the first player in WNBA history to record a double-double in her first three Finals games.

With the game level at 49-49 in the third quarter, Atlanta scored eight straight, including four by Reese. Golden State got within 59-55 on Tiffany Hayes' layup, but could get no closer as Atlanta closed the quarter scoring 12 of the final 14 points.

Atlanta have dominated the third quarter so far in the series, outscoring Golden State 63-35 combined in the three games.

With Atlanta up 17 in the fourth quarter, Jordin Canada overthrew Reese on the break, but she saved the ball by throwing it over her head underneath the basket to Howard, who got fouled.

Golden State could never recover. Gabby Williams scored 15 points and Hayes added 14 for the Valkyries.

This game was originally scheduled to be played on Thursday at the Gateway Center Arena, where the Dream play most of their home games. The league was able to work with the Atlanta Hawks and State Farm Arena to play the next two games of the championship series there so that they could have a much bigger crowd. Gateway only seats 3,500 while State Farm Arena can seat more than 17,000 fans.

Wednesday night's game was sold out as is Game 4 on Saturday, which will also be played at State Farm Arena.

The game got off to a slow start as Atlanta led 9-1 after the first five minutes. Golden State missed its first eight shots before Aminata Gueye scored the first basket for the Valkyries with 4:39 left. They got within 13-10 before Naz Hillmon hit consecutive three-pointers and then Reese hit one. The Dream led 23-15 after the opening quarter.

The hot three-point shooting continued in the second quarter as Atlanta built its lead to 37-26 midway through the period. Golden State was able to hang around and only trailed 46-40 at the break as the teams combined to shoot 15-for-31 (48 per cent) from behind the arc. That was more made 3-pointers in the first 20 minutes then in either Game 1 or Game 2.

articles.title: A qué hora es el Maccabi Tel Aviv - Real Madrid: horario y dónde ver hoy en TV el partido de la Euroliga
articles.standfirst: Partido de la jornada 7 de la Euroliga
articles.summary: Partido de la jornada 7 de la Euroliga
articles.body: Después de tres derrotas consecutivas en el arranque, el Madrid ha logrado enderezar su rumbo en la Euroliga con otras tres victorias seguidas, equilibrando su balance primero y sobre todo llevando cierta estabilidad al proyecto. Esas victorias más las cuatro de Liga Endesa (donde es líder en solitario) hacen pensar que la nace que dirige Pedro Martínez empieza a transitar con velocidad de crucero. Y hay momentos muy brillantes en su juego. Los blancos rinden visita al Maccabi que como ya es sabido no juega en Tel Aviv, sino en Belgrado, en el Aleksandar Nikolic Hall (la antigua sala Pionir) y a puerta cerrada, no suelen ir más de 300 o 400 invitados. Eso hace que los israelíes sean más vulnerables en casa que si jugaran en su, otrora casi inexpugnable, Menora Mivtachim Arena en Tel Aviv. Con una victoria menos que los blancos, el Maccabi luce un balance de 2-4. Lo más normal, por plantilla, química y opciones, es que el Maccabi acabe fuera de los puestos de Playoffs y, como mucho si se la da bien la temporada, luche por meter la cabeza en el Play-In. Pero no es un equipo fácil y viene, en doble jornada, de llevar al límite al Barça, que ganó sobre la bocina con un triple de Robinson, y de ganar al Valencia en el Roig Arena. Ls israelíes tendrán la baja de Lundberg, con rotura parcial del tendón del cuádriceps, y que se espera que esté fuera entre seis y ocho semanas. En el Madrid, sólo las bajas ya conocidas y de larga duración de Usman Garuba y Gabi Deck. El encuentro entre el Maccabi Tel Aviv y el Real Madrid, correspondiente a la séptima jornada de la Euroliga, se disputa este jueves 22 de octubre a las 20.05 horas (horario peninsular español) en el Aleksandar Nikolic Hall de Belgrado. articles.standfirst: Yaxel Lendeborg, rookie de los Warriors, tuvo un acalorado duelo con la estrella de los Lakers, al que criticó duramente
articles.summary: Yaxel Lendeborg, rookie de los Warriors, tuvo un acalorado duelo con la estrella de los Lakers, al que criticó duramente
articles.body: Luka Doncic tiene un nuevo enemigo en la NBA. Se trata de Yaxel Lendeborg, alero novato de los Warriors. Los dos se enfrentaron en el primer partido de la temporada de sus respectivos equipos y saltaron chispas. Hubo piques, palabras subidas de tono y las declaraciones continuaron al finalizar el encuentro. "Le tenía mucho respeto porque no veía mucho la NBA, sólo los mejores momentos y lo veía arrasar con sus rivales. Pero al estar en primera persona y ver todas sus quejas y lamentos, le perdí todo el respeto", aseguró el rookie, excompañero de Aday Mara en la Universidad de Míchigan, sobre la estrella de los Lakers. El asunto se calentó en los últimos minutos del segundo cuarto, cuando a Lendeborg le señalaron una personal sobre Doncic que él consideraba que no había cometido. "No me frustré por la falta que le pitaron, sino porque él se estuvo quejando durante todo el partido", comentó el jugador de los Warriors, que consiguió minimizar los recursos del base de los Lakers. Según datos de ESPN, hizo 1/6 en tiros cuando fue su defensor principal. Tras una de esas buenas acciones defensivas, a Lendeborg le señalaron una técnica por gritar a su rival. "Le estaba diciendo que era un inútil. No puede anotarme. Habla mucho, pero no puede anotarme. Lo dije durante todo el partido. Obviamente, dije algunas palabrotas. Por eso me pitaron la falta técnica, pero se lo estaba dejando claro", contó después del partido. "Estaba diciendo tonterías, pero yo intentaba no responderle. Esta temporada no busco que me piten faltas técnicas", aseguró Doncic, que se vengó al final de la primera parte con un triple a tablero desde medio campo. Por supuesto, hubo comentarios hacia el novato. "Se le encaró y eso también debería haber sido técnica", se quejó Steve Kerr, entrenador de los Warriors. "Supongo que así es la NBA. Muchas simulaciones, muchas faltas provocadas, muchas quejas a los árbitros. Un primer partido interesante para mí", resumió Lendeborg, que tuvo un agitado estreno en la competición, aunque por su carácter no parece un novato al uso. Hay que tener valor para picarse con Doncic en tu primera noche en la Liga.

The coach added that the alleged failed test was kept "a secret" from the rest of the team. The allegation also appears in Batie-Smooseâs Oct. 13 federal lawsuit against the California State University (CSU) trustees and 11 SJSU employees. Fleming then missed a long stretch of the 2023 season. SJSUâs athletics website claimed the player had not competed since Sept. 16 of that year "due to injuries," in a November 2023 game recap. Batie-Smoose said, "The injury happened the day that Fleming went to go get tested, and it was very questionable." In 2023, NCAA rules allowed transgender women to play on womenâs teams, but they had to meet requirements for hormone treatment and testosterone levels. The NCAA kept that policy, known as Phase Two, in place through the 2023â24 school year. Under that framework, transgender women had to complete at least one year of testosterone suppression treatment before competing on a womenâs team. They also had to provide blood-test results that met the NCAAâs limit for their sport. For womenâs volleyball, the Phase Two limit was below 10 nanomoles per liter of total testosterone in the blood. The requirements applied before an athleteâs first competition in each season segment, including nonconference games. Schools had to submit eligibility documents for an NCAA medical panel to review before the athlete competed. The requirement did not begin only when conference play started. She also says her relationship with head coach Todd Kress unraveled as their political views grew apart â and accuses him of using her support for Trump to turn players against her. She described Kress as a longtime friend who once shared her conservative beliefs. "Todd was a conservative Republican, and we shared the same views on a lot of things. And thatâs why we were friends for so long," she said. "And then somewhere in the craziness, he went left and really extreme left." Asked when she noticed that change, Batie-Smoose said it happened "before the first Trump election." The two continued discussing politics, she said. "We can talk and debate on those subjects when weâre in a room together, but not in front of student athletes. I feel like that is not the time and the place to speak on that." She alleged that Kress knew which players would object to her views and raised the subject in front of them to create division. Her lawsuit alleges that Kress called her a "Trump lover." It also says she repeatedly expressed her religious belief that "God made man and woman," and that she believes his treatment reflected hostility toward her faith. She further alleges that he cornered and berated her during an office confrontation in about August 2023, after a canceled recruiting visit. The complaint says he threatened that he could get her fired. Batie-Smoose says she reported the encounter to administrators and human resources. articles.title: Ranking the Top 10 Realistic NBA Trade Targets This Season
articles.summary: The NBA trade market might be dormant at the moment, but it can awaken at any time.
articles.body:
The NBA trade market might be dormant at the moment, but it can awaken at any time.

And as soon as it does, it is capable of immediately impacting the league's balance of power.

Because, from our vantage point, this year's pool of realistic (or at least logical) trade candidates runs deep with potential difference-makers. From sharpshooters to stoppers, from rising stars to future Hall of Famers, this player pool is capable of scratching virtually any itch.

Without knowing what's ahead of all 30 teams, we are applying a liberal definition of the word realistic, but we're still focused on players who either have been mentioned in trade buzz or have a reasonable path to get there. Then, we're ranking these 10 players based on possible trade value, weighing everything from age and ability to contract commitments and ease of adjustment to a midseason move.

Chicago's two-year, $45 million pact with Norman Powell felt like a short-term arrangement from the moment he signed it this summer. It carries a team option on the second season, for starters, so the Bulls have an easy way out of this if it's obvious the pairing just doesn't work.

In a perfect world, though, Powell will play well, impart veteran know-how to his young teammates and attract a host of win-now suitors between now and the deadline. He is not at all a timeline fit for this rebuilder, but he could be a great plug-and-play option for a team in need of a scoring boost.

His peak has arrived later than most, but it's here now, and it's pretty awesome. He has netted better than 21 points per night each of the past two seasons, compiling a 47.7/40/81.6 shooting slash over this stretch. He also debuted as an All-Star in 2025-26.

There were some rumblings about Brooklyn aiming to accelerate this season, but things didn't really materialize. Sure, they added Julius Randle, but they sacrificed their starting center (Nic Claxton) and gained a first-round pick in the exchange.

Their future still holds more intrigue than their present with recent top-10 picks Egor Dëmin (No. 8 in 2025) and Mikel Brown Jr. (No. 6 in 2026) hopefully ushering in that next chapter.

If the Nets, losers of 118 games over the past two seasons, aren't dramatically more competitive, they should be aiming to flip Michael Porter Jr. for long-term assets.

Dubbed a "player to watch" in trade talks by ESPN's Brian Windhorst , Porter has an expiring contract, a coveted (and translatable) skill set as a perimeter sharpshooter and high-stakes playoff experience from his days in Denver.

Porter is overpaid ( $40.8 million ), and his numbers with the Nets (24.2 points per game) overstate his overall impact, but he'd still boost any offense struggling with spacing and secondary scoring.

The Blazers have too many guards to maximize their talent base.

There just aren't enough touches to go around in an offense featuring Jrue Holiday, Damian Lillard, Ja Morant, Scoot Henderson and Shaedon Sharpe, especially when considering that star swingman Deni Avdija works best on the ball, too.

Someone—or perhaps more than one player—is getting squeezed out of the Pacific Northwest, and Holiday could be the odd man out. His best days are behind him, but he still provides value through his intelligence and versatility on defense and his ability to contribute on or off the ball offensively.

Holiday has been productive with all five of his NBA employers, so he knows how to navigate a scenery change. He also shouldn't cost a ton in trade assets since he is set to collect $72 million over his age-36 and -37 seasons.

Anthony Davis and the Wizards are taking a wait-and-see approach with any contract extension talks, which makes sense for myriad reasons.

They both have plenty to learn about one another, like how Davis looks after being limited to just 20 appearances last season and how close Washington is to competing on the heels of three consecutive 64-plus-loss campaigns.

This wait could also be huge for Davis' possible trade suitors, since they'll want reassurance about both his two-way impact and his availability.

As one Western Conference executive told ESPN's Brian Windhorst , Davis is "going to be playing for a contract or maybe playing to get traded," so he'll be incentivized to be at his best.

From a strictly talent-based perspective, Davis ranks favorably among all players on this list, but a few things hold back his ranking. His availability concerns, for one, are...well, concerning, as he has reached 60 games in just one of the past six seasons. He's also owed a boatload of money ($58.5 million this season with a $62.8 million player option for 2027-28) and reportedly has hopes of securing another max commitment .

The Mavericks might be genuine in their stated desire to keep Kyrie Irving around, and his connection with Dallas may be pure and authentic.

None of that will stop trade speculation, since none of that can bridge the timeline gap between the 34-year-old point guard and the franchise's 19-year-old centerpiece, Cooper Flagg.

"If [Irving] comes back healthy for a significant sample size that shows every other team around the NBA that he is still capable of being an All-Star talent and a playoff game-changer especially as a halfcourt ball-handling creator, the Mavs, I believe, are going to get trade offers that ultimately they are not going to be able to refuse," Jake Fischer said on a Bleacher Report live stream.

"They can keep saying right now and projecting publicly and saying it behind the scenes that they are not interested in moving him, but things do change very very quickly in the NBA."

As Fischer noted, Irving needs to prove himself a bit after missing the last season-plus with a torn ACL. Even when he does, his age and uncertain future (player option for 2027-28) will limit his market a bit.

That said, any win-now shopper hoping for more offensive oomph might make him their top priority.

Admittedly, there aren't direct trade winds swirling around Darius Garland at the moment. Still, it doesn't take much dot-connecting to see how they could get moving.

The Clippers have no hopes of contending any time soon, but their future might be even bleaker after the NBA ordered them to forfeit five first-round picks following its salary-cap circumvention investigation . The team has disputed the findings and said it would challenge them. L.A. may want to scoop up assets wherever it can find some, and no one on its roster would deliver more than Garland.

He'd sit higher up this list without availability concerns or defensive limitations, but they don't change the fact that he's a two-time All-Star with a knockdown three-point shot and a wealth of offensive creativity off the bounce.

Garland wouldn't be the easiest player for every team to add since he needs the offensive keys to thrive, but he does up his market appeal by fitting both win-now and win-soon suitors.

Kevin Durant feels virtually impossible to rank here.

A number of factors play into that, starting with the fact that Houston probably has no interest in giving him up. Then again, if the Rockets can't get off the launching pad and into the West's top tier by the deadline, they probably need to choose between going all-in on a co-star for Durant or trading Durant to reset their timeline around their young core.

If Houston seems outside of the inner circle of contenders, there may not be a midseason move to make to gain entry. So, Durant has a realistic chance of surfacing in trade talks again.

Who would want him? Great question. On the one hand, he is a generational scorer with the kind of game that fits any system. On the other, front offices might be wary of some of the messier exits in his past, and he isn't young (38), cheap ( $43.9 million salary ) or guaranteed to stick around past this season (player option for 2027-28).

There is an argument to be made that of all the players ranked here, Franz Wagner might be the toughest to pry loose—for now.

But that might all go out the window if Orlando struggles out of the gate and quickly concludes that its offseason coaching change (Jamahl Mosley out, Sean Sweeney in) wasn't enough to lift this core's first-round ceiling.

The Magic have struggled to maximize star wings Wagner and Paolo Banchero together, and their shared on-ball strengths and off-ball weaknesses (both sub-33 percent three-point shooters) might prevent it from ever happening.

At 25 years old, Wagner perhaps hasn't reached his peak, which is an exciting thought for someone with this much size (6'10", 220 lbs) and skill.

That said, he has had trouble staying on the court of late (94 games over the past two seasons), he could be prohibitively expensive in both trade assets and salary , and teams with ball-dominant stars could wonder whether they'd encounter some of the same issues he's had fitting with Banchero.

Maybe we're not indulging in enough October optimism, but things could really spiral if the Magic get off to a slow start.

After paying such a heavy premium for Desmond Bane last offseason, they can't really afford another huge addition. Their most consequential remaining option could be a substantial subtraction.

"Every player on the payroll could be considered a trade candidate if the team does not get off to a fast start," Heavy.com's Sean Deveney wrote of the Magic.

Financially speaking, Paolo Banchero could be tricky to move, since he's just starting a five-year, $239.2 million deal . At the same time, teams rarely have a chance to trade for someone this young (24 in November), this well-regarded (No. 1 pick in 2022) and this productive (career 22.3 points, 7.4 rebounds and 4.8 assists).

He would need an offensive system tailored around him, but a system with better spacing than Orlando's could launch him toward superstar status. Not everyone can afford that lottery ticket, and some that can won't bother to try, but the teams that do want Banchero would really want him.

1. Trey Murphy III, New Orleans Pelicans

These rankings feature players who have earned some of the league's highest honors. Trey Murphy III's main distinction through five NBA seasons has been…finishing second in the 2023 Slam Dunk Contest, maybe?

So, how does he claim the No. 1 spot? Because we're measuring trade value, and Murphy's stands taller than the rest due to his blend of perhaps universal appeal (young enough for even rebuilders to target, established enough to convince contenders he has instant-impact ability), a wholly reasonable pay rate (three years, $87 million ) and a wealth of supplemental skills that could be easily integrated into any kind of system.

The Pelicans, of course, want a fortune in return for Murphy. Per HoopsHype's Michael Scotto , the asking price this summer was "the equivalent of...three first-round picks." In that same report, Scotto identified five different teams as being "in the mix for Murphy." In other words, that steep cost isn't scaring folks away.

Murphy really is the ideal trade candidate on the market right now. He feasts on an analytically friendly shot diet of powerful dunks and long-range threes, holds his own as a versatile defender and fits into virtually any budget or system. He isn't the biggest name on this list, but his trade value is unrivaled.

articles.title: 7 NBA Players Who Can Be First-Time All-Stars
articles.summary: Last year saw a remarkable six players make their first NBA All-Star appearances, so we decided to embrace optimism by highlighting seven who could do the same in 2026-27.
articles.body:
Last year saw a remarkable six players make their first NBA All-Star appearances, so we decided to embrace optimism by highlighting seven who could do the same in 2026-27.

The previous season's field of first-timers—Deni Avdija, Jalen Duren, Chet Holmgren, Jalen Johnson, Jamal Murray and Norman Powell—is instructive, populated mostly by players in their early 20s, but with some established vets sprinkled in.

The takeaway: It's never too early or too late to make a leap.

From second-year studs like Cooper Flagg and Dylan Harper to 30-something role-players like Derrick White, first-time All-Star candidates can come in all shapes, ages and sizes. Let's dig into the upcoming season's breakthrough crew.

Shooting percentages aside, Cooper Flagg's stats were probably good enough to earn him an All-Star nod last season. Teenager or not, averages of 21.0 points, 6.7 rebounds, 4.5 assists, 1.2 steals and 0.9 blocks were eye-opening.

Flagg will need to do better than 29.5 percent from deep, which should be within his abilities if Kyrie Irving is able to lighten some of the ball-handling load. Maybe new head coach Dusty May will also look to draw up more schemes that allow Flagg to use his speed, power and cutting acumen to get some easy looks around the basket.

In addition to potential efficiency gains, Flagg should also be in line to meet expectations as a defender. That's not typically the kind of thing that leads to All-Star berths, but Flagg fell way short of the defensive impact many anticipated from him coming out of Duke. Though disappointing, it was hardly his fault. Dallas burdened him with a massive offensive job that sapped his physical and mental energy.

At the very least, a more reasonable role for Flagg could produce more highlight defensive plays and wins, earning attention and votes.

It's not easy for sophomores to make the All-Star Game, and it's even tougher for those that'll play the first two months of the season at age 19. But Flagg seems like a special talent. If anyone's going to buck trends, it'll be him.

The Los Angeles Lakers' $180 million investment in Austin Reaves comes with All-Star-level expectations.

The five-year veteran probably would have had a shot to earn his first nod if he hadn't gone down for the better part of six weeks in mid-December with a calf strain. Up through Dec. 10, he was averaging 27.8 points, 6.7 assists and 5.6 rebounds on a 50.3/36.9/87.5 shooting split.

During that season-opening surge, Reaves looked very much like a first-option superstar whenever he had to carry the load without Luka Dončić or LeBron James.

Dončić is back with the Lakers, but James isn't. That should mean more touches and opportunities for Reaves, doubly so if Luka can't stay healthy.

Smack in the middle of his prime at age 28, Reaves' career has featured flashes of exceptional three-point shooting, primary-playmaker facilitation and a ton of self-sufficient scoring skill. If he puts all of that together in 2026-27, he'll join Dončić as an All-Star.

If Franz Wagner slips back below 30.0 percent from three, his first-time All-Star case will become much harder to make.

But if we journey back to the first 25 games of 2024-25, which might be the last time Franz Wagner was fully healthy, there's reason to believe that a) his jumper hasn't always been busted, and b) he's long overdue for an All-Star trip.

Wagner was basically an All-NBA first-teamer through early December 2024, averaging 24.4 points, 5.7 assists and 5.6 rebounds while hitting a borderline respectable 32.1 percent of his 6.4 deep attempts per game.

Injuries struck, Wagner missed almost two months, and he wasn't the same upon returning. Last year was another injury-marred mess, but he managed to hit 34.5 percent of his threes in 34 games.

Between his first two years of roughly league-average shooting, the flashes of stardom he showed in 2024-25 and a career free-throw percentage of 85.1 percent, Wagner has plenty of positive indicators. He'll always be a handful going downhill, he can pass the ball and is in the early part of his prime at 25.

If he can iron out the hitch in his long-range shot, Wagner is going to perform at least as well as he did during that career-best stretch two seasons ago. As long as the Orlando Magic are playing winning ball by the time voting concludes, that should be enough to earn Wagner his All-Star debut.

Every NBA Team's Top 3 Trade Targets This Season 🎯

NBA Stars with Most on the Line This Season 🫡

If Jaden McDaniels makes his first All-Star team, there's a good chance that basically everything will have gone right for the Minnesota Timberwolves during the first half of the season.

A nod for him would probably mean LaMelo Ball delivered the exact kind of teammate-lifting facilitation the Wolves expected, so much so that McDaniels would join him and Anthony Edwards in the All-Star game. If Minnesota sends three representatives to Phoenix, it'll almost certainly have to be near the top of the West standings.

McDaniels' defense has been elite for years, and he's tantalized with postseason flashes of self-sufficient work on offense more than once. With Julius Randle gone and Ball tending to generate great looks for his teammates, McDaniels could be in for elevated shot quantity and quality.

Just 26 years old, coming off three straight years of improved scoring averages and already generating a ton of preseason hype , McDaniels has virtually every "potential leap" factor working in his favor.

The cosmetic stats—23.6 points and 6.1 assists—were there last year, but Keyonte George can make them count for something if he produces similarly on a Utah Jazz team that actually wins some games.

He can do that this season as Utah shifts its focus toward winning.

George is a threat to hit pull-up threes, and that threshold skill unlocks all the other valuable aspects of his offensive game. Because defenders have to worry about him beyond the arc (37.1 percent last season), George is often positioned to attack opponents who are leaning toward him in fear of his jumper.

George is quick off the dribble and can get into space easily, which is how he piled up 7.0 free-throw attempts per game last year. In addition to developing his craft as a foul-drawer, George is also adept at flipping in runners and floaters. If he chooses to give the ball up rather than challenge at the rim, his lob game makes him a threat as a passer.

The Jazz could put several names into the All-Star hat this season, including Lauri Markkanen and Jaren Jackson Jr. George, a potential first-timer, might be the team's most worthy representative.

Though teammate Stephon Castle has the edge in experience (by a year) and amassed superior counting stats that owed to his larger starting role last season, Dylan Harper is the Spurs guard with the highest upside.

The lefty was San Antonio's second-best player during long stretches of the 2026 postseason, flashing every element you'd want to see from a future first-option shot creator. Quickness, craft, creativity, force around the basket, vision—it was all there on the biggest stage.

There's just no chance Harper's development will slow down as he enters his second season. Give him the minutes, and he'll outproduce both Castle and De'Aaron Fox.

Do you know how many 19-year-olds have averaged at least 18.0 points, 6.0 assists and 5.0 rebounds per 36 while posting a true shooting percentage north of 57.0 percent? Just one: Harper.

Do you know how many of those players went on to make an All-Star appearance at age 20?

OK, so far: zero. That's about to change, though.

I, for one, refuse to believe Derrick White forgot how to shoot a basketball.

Last year's percentages (39.4 percent overall and 32.7 percent from long range) would beg to differ, but it's going to take more than one outlier to cause any real alarm.

White is entering his age-32 season, which certainly raises the specter of athletic decline. But shooting? No way. Expect the veteran guard to come much closer to the form he showed in his first three full years with Boston, when he hit 38.1, 39.6 and 38.4 percent of his threes, respectively.

With Jaylen Brown gone, White could also see a higher share of shots and playmaking duties. If he continues to rate as one of the best catch-all-metric players in the sport, gets his three-point shooting back to its previous level and does both for a Boston Celtics team near the top of the East when voting concludes, you've got a recipe for a late-career All-Star debut.

articles.title: Giannis Antetokounmpo reportedly invested $70 million in apartment buildings from October 2025 as his property business expanded
articles.summary: Giannis Antetokounmpo has put roughly $70 million into apartment buildings since October 2025, according to reports on his family company.
articles.body: Giannis Antetokounmpo has put roughly $70 million into apartment buildings since October 2025, according to reports on his family company. Ante, launched in 2023 by Antetokounmpo with his brothers Thanasis, Kostas and Alex, handled the deals. The purchases cover 186 units across Wisconsin, Brooklyn and Chicago. The newest big spend is personal. A company linked to the Miami Heat forward paid $13.5 million for a mansion in Pinecrest, Florida, in early September, after the Milwaukee Bucks traded the two-time MVP to Miami.How did Giannis Antetokounmpo’s $70 million real estate run start?The buying began in October 2025 with The Atwater, a 39-unit building in Shorewood, Wisconsin, bought for $11.75 million. A month later, Ante added The Emerson, a 41-unit building in Madison, for $11.6 million. Both sit in the state where the Bucks play.The biggest single move came in Brooklyn. Ante paid about $25.2 million for two neighboring buildings in Prospect Lefferts Gardens, known together as The Lawrence. They hold 50 apartments. Chicago followed with a $21 million purchase, covered in a later section.Add the four deals and the total lands near $69.6 million. That matches the figure CoStar first reported for Antetokounmpo’s family office, more than $69 million in about a year. The spending covers five buildings and 186 units.Ante is not a one-purpose company. It started as a vehicle to manage business ventures, investments and brand holdings around the world, and real estate is one piece of that. In 2024 the group also launched Improbable Media, a production and brand strategy company co-founded with former NBA guard and ESPN analyst Jay Williams.Purchase prices do not equal cash spent, since loans can cover part of a deal. The Chicago building, for one, came with an $11 million loan.What do we know about Antetokounmpo’s $13.5 million Miami mansion?A company linked to the two-time MVP paid $13.5 million for the house in Pinecrest, a village about 11 miles southwest of downtown Miami. The Real Deal reported the sale from property records. The buyer is an entity tied to the player’s attorneys in New York, and its name follows the same style as other companies Antetokounmpo uses.The listing describes a nearly 12,000-square-foot home with eight bedrooms, 10 bathrooms and two half-bathrooms. It sits on just over an acre, is not on the water and was recently completed. Inside are a media room and a guest house, and the grounds have a pool and Jacuzzi. Listing photos also show a covered outdoor kitchen and bar, poolside lounge areas and a second-level sky terrace. Total space reaches more than 15,000 square feet when indoor and outdoor areas are counted.The asking price was $16.3 million, so the buyer saved $2.8 million at closing. A company led by Fouad Kraishan sold the property, with Juan Annicchiarico of JCAS Realty representing the seller. Ignacio Permuy of Coral Gables-based Permuy Architecture designed it. The lot is north of Deering Bay and west of Gables by the Sea.Why do so many NBA players buy homes in Pinecrest?Larger lots, more privacy and a short drive to private schools explain much of the pull. Pinecrest and nearby South Miami have housed athletes and celebrities for years.The neighbors show how crowded the NBA list is. Tyler Herro, sent to Milwaukee in the same trade, listed his Pinecrest mansion across the street from Antetokounmpo’s for nearly $12 million on the day the deal was finalized in July. Herro paid $10.5 million for it in late 2022. Jeff Green sold his Pinecrest house for $15.5 million in April. Two years ago Jimmy Butler sold a 6,148-square-foot, six-bedroom home near South Miami and Coral Gables for $8.3 million, and Dion Waiters sold his Pinecrest home the same year.Against those sales, the $13.5 million price sits above what Herro paid and below what Green got. The village record for a single-family sale is $19.5 million, set last year, so the Heat star’s purchase falls well short of that mark.Antetokounmpo’s family company spends $21 million in ChicagoAnte paid more than $21 million for Harmony Apartments, a four-story building on Chicago’s North Side. It was completed in 2024 and holds 56 units. The building sits roughly 85 miles from Fiserv Forum, where Antetokounmpo played his home games as a Buck.Essex Realty Group handled the sale. Old National Bank provided an $11 million loan, which means about half the price was financed. Ante is founded and run by Antetokounmpo and brothers Thanasis, Kostas and Alex, and the Chicago deal was the fourth in the run after two in Wisconsin and one in Brooklyn.It also brought the unit count to 186 across the portfolio. Of the $69.6 million spent on apartments, Chicago made up close to a third.How much is Antetokounmpo worth, and what has the NBA paid so far?Estimates put Antetokounmpo’s net worth at $170 million, with a listed salary of $58 million. Career NBA earnings total $335.2 million across 13 seasons with Milwaukee.The pay climbed fast. A rookie deal paid $1.8 million in 2013-14. A four-year, $100 million contract followed in September 2016. In December 2020 Antetokounmpo signed a five-year, $228 million extension, the largest deal in NBA history at the time. Another extension arrived in October 2023, worth $186 million over three years. Salary reached $51.9 million in 2025-26. Endorsements add at least $10 million a year, including a long-term Nike deal signed in November 2017.The production matched the money. Milwaukee drafted the forward 15th in 2013. Two MVP awards came in 2019 and 2020, then the 2021 title, when Antetokounmpo scored 50 points in the clinching Game 6 and won Finals MVP. Last season the Bucks went 32-50 and missed the playoffs while Antetokounmpo played 36 games, averaging 27.6 points, 9.8 rebounds and 5.4 assists.Set against the $170 million estimate, the $70 million in apartment deals equals about 40 percent. articles.title: Warriors, Heat, More on Wrong Side of NBA History With Rare Stat After Blowout Losses in Openers
articles.summary: Most of the NBA opened their regular-season schedules on Wednesday night, and the slate turned out to be historically one-sided.
articles.body:
Most of the NBA opened their regular-season schedules on Wednesday night, and the slate turned out to be historically one-sided.

According to OptaStats, six teams lost their season openers by 20 or more points on Wednesday, marking the first time that has ever happened in the same season:

Two of those teams fell by more than 40 points, as the Toronto Raptors destroyed the Chicago Bulls 135-92 and the Portland Trail Blazers dominated the Phoenix Suns 124-83.

Perhaps the two most interesting teams on the list are perennial playoff contenders in the Miami Heat and Golden State Warriors.

There was a ton of excitement surrounding Miami's home opener against the Minnesota Timberwolves since it marked superstar forward Giannis Antetokounmpo's regular-season debut with the Heat.

The Heat were overwhelmed in a 25-points loss to the Minnesota Timberwolves, though, as Anthony Edwards led all scorers with 45 points in Minnesota's 131-106 road victory.

Giannis played well in his own right with 35 points, but none of his teammates scored more than 15, which is undoubtedly something head coach Erik Spoelstra will hope doesn't become a trend.

As for the Warriors, they entered the season shorthanded with Jimmy Butler still out of the lineup while recovering from a torn ACL, and Kristaps Porziņģis on the shelf as he continues to deal with a long-running illness.

Golden State still had holdovers such as Stephen Curry and Draymond Green, but it wasn't enough to overcome a Los Angeles Lakers team that rolled to a 127-105 win at home.

Much like Giannis, Curry was something of a one-man show, scoring 23 points, while no other Warriors player scored more than 14 points.

Three Lakers players scored 23 or more points, though, led by Luka Doncic, who paced the game with 28 points to go along with eight rebounds and seven assists.

articles.title: ‘Is this political?’ – Enes Kanter demands meeting with Adam Silver over WNBA
articles.summary: Enes Kanter Freedom is taking his fight straight to the top, demanding a meeting with Adam Silver. Enes Kanter’s feud with the WNBA has only gotten messier l...
articles.body:
Enes Kanter Freedom is taking his fight straight to the top, demanding a meeting with Adam Silver.

Enes Kanter's feud with the WNBA has only gotten messier lately. After mockingly announcing he was going to enter the WNBA Draft to make a point about women's sports, league commissioner Cathy Engelbert shut that down, ruling him completely ineligible.

The drama peaked once again after showing up for Game 3 of the WNBA Finals in Atlanta. Venue security tried to put him in a private suite for safety reasons, but Kanter refused, insisting on sitting in the floor seats he paid for. When he wouldn't budge, police turned him away entirely.

Enes Kanter wants answers from Adam Silver

Enes Kanter is taking his fight straight to the top, demanding a sit-down with Adam Silver after claiming WNBA officials completely ignored him.

The former center wants to grill the commissioner on the league's political direction, arguing Silver owes him answers since the NBA heavily subsidises the operation.

On the Sage Steele Show , he said: "I think I'm going to request a meeting with Adam Silver because I know they're the one that paying the bills. So I'm going to request a meeting with Silver. I mean, as a former player, he should take the meeting. Yeah, I think it is important because I did try to have a meeting with the WNBA and the WB players, the player association for women, but they didn't get back to us or me."

"I want to know what you guys are thinking. I would put them in a corner or anything. I was just like, tell me what you're thinking. I want to know your mindset. I want to know like what do you what are you planning to do? Is this like a is this a political thing that you guys are doing right before the midterms? Like what are you guys thinking about doing?"

Adam Silver isn't likely to budge on Enes Kanter Freedom's demands. NBA and arena security handled his seating dispute at the WNBA Finals, so they're not suddenly going to have a different opinion.

Silver won't let Kanter dictate the narrative or force a meeting on his own terms.

articles.title: 'He Sucks,' Yaxel Lendeborg Rips Luka Doncic in Video After Warriors-Lakers, 'Lost All Respect'
articles.summary: Among the many things Luka Dončić has been known for throughout his NBA career is complaining about the officiating during games, something Yaxel Lendeborg experience in his first game as the Los Angeles Lakers defeated the Golden State Warriors 127-105 on Wednesday night.
articles.body:
Among the many things Luka Dončić has been known for throughout his NBA career is complaining about the officiating during games, something Yaxel Lendeborg experience in his first game as the Los Angeles Lakers defeated the Golden State Warriors 127-105 on Wednesday night.

Lendeborg told reporters afterward he "lost all respect" for Dončić because he was "complaining the entire game" before adding he told the Lakers star "he sucks" at one point when they were on the floor together.

One key source of Lendeborg's frustration was likely a sequence in the second quarter when Dončić pump-faked the Warriors rookie into a foul, then proceeded to chirp at him about it after the two had been playing physical throughout the game.

Asked about the back-and-forth with Lendeborg from his perspective (starts at :51 mark), Dončić said the Warriors forward was "talking crazy" and he "wasn't trying to talk back" because he's "not trying to get techs."

Lendeborg, the No. 11 pick in the 2026 draft, was matched up frequently on Dončić since the Warriors are still without Jimmy Butler and Moses Moody due to injuries.

Dončić put up 28 points, eight rebounds and seven assists, but Lendeborg actually did a good job as the primary defender against the six-time All-Star.

Dončić's knack for complaining during games is so notorious that even he has acknowledged at times it probably goes too far. It hasn't actually stopped him from doing it, but why would it when he does get calls.

Since his rookie season in 2018-19, Dončić ranks third among all players with 8.5 free-throw attempts per game.

The bad news for Lendeborg is he tossed this quote out after his first game, giving Dončić plenty of fuel to use the next time the Lakers and Warriors meet.

We won't have to wait long to see what happens. The Warriors will host the Lakers at Chase Center on Oct. 30.

articles.title: ‘I lost all respect’: Warriors rookie blasts Lakers star Luka Doncic after blowout loss
articles.summary: Yaxel Lendeborg has only played one NBA game, yet he’s already started a feisty feud with Luka Doncic.
articles.body: LOS ANGELES — Yaxel Lendeborg has only played one NBA game, yet he’s already started a feisty feud with Luka Doncic. The Golden State Warriors rookie began his career Wednesday night by refusing to back down from the reigning NBA scoring champion, who punctuated their prolonged on-court exchange of trash talk by making a spectacular half-court shot in Lendeborg’s face at the halftime buzzer. Doncic also won this fight decisively on the scoreboard when the Los Angeles Lakers blew out Lendeborg and the Warriors 127-105, with Doncic scoring 28 points in just three quarters. Yet Lendeborg somehow wasn’t finished talking: He called out the six-time All-Star as a complainer and a free-throw merchant during his postgame news conference. “I lost all respect (for Doncic), man,” Lendeborg said. “That was awful. ... A lot of flopping, a lot of foul-baiting, a lot of praying to the ref, man. Interesting first game for me, for sure.” The Warriors’ 24-year-old rookie first-round pick said he sparred with Doncic on the court because of the Slovenian superstar’s constant complaining to the officials — admittedly a common feature of most games in Doncic’s nine-year career. Lendeborg, who won an NCAA title with Michigan last season, said he enjoyed watching highlights of Doncic’s electric scoring performances in the past — but he has a more jaded perspective on Doncic’s skills now. “Me getting frustrated, it’s not about the foul being called,” Lendeborg said. “It’s about him complaining the entire game, and then you get the foul call, and congratulations, bro. And then you talk to me like you did something great? Bro, come on. That’s just weak, you know? It kind of threw me off for a little while, because like I said, I had so much respect for him. Gone, man. Gone.” Lendeborg and Doncic exchanged insults for much of the second quarter, with Lendeborg being whistled for a technical foul after saying something so loud and profane it caught the officials’ attention. “I was telling him he sucks,” Lendeborg said with a smile. “‘You can’t score on me.’ I said it the whole game. I said a couple of cuss words, obviously. That’s why I got the technical and all that, but I was letting him know, because he was laughing and talking, all this because of that one foul call.” Doncic mostly laughed off Lendeborg’s provocations, but the Lakers star obviously thrives amid confrontation. He was whistled for 16 technical fouls last season, earning a one-game suspension for exceeding the single-season limit. “He was talking crazy, but I wasn’t trying to talk back this season,” Doncic said of Lendeborg. “Not trying to get techs. For the first time, that was not a double tech, because I didn’t say nothing, so I’m working on it. As you see, I think it worked great.” Doncic got the ultimate victory at the final buzzer — but his halftime win was incredibly sweet as well. “I knew that was going in before I got it in my hands,” Doncic said with a grin. “I work on those.” He got the ball near the scorer’s table and let it fly with nearly 3 seconds left on the clock. When it banked through and set off pandemonium in the Lakers’ downtown arena, Doncic gleefully pointed at the fuming Lendeborg, who wasn’t impressed. “His only bucket on me was a banker from half court,” Lendeborg said. “I know it’s a team sport. He had 28 on us as a team. Me, I took my matchup personally. Tried not to get called on the fouls. Tried my best. I was thinking about playing him with my hands behind my back to see if that worked. Probably would have still got a foul call. But interesting.” A Warriors official then steered Lendeborg away from further denigrating one of the greatest players in modern basketball, but the rookie had already done more than enough to stoke this burgeoning personal feud as a fascinating new addition to these California teams’ historic rivalry. Doncic and Lendeborg should see each other again on Oct. 30, when the Lakers visit San Francisco.
